tldr: In humanoid whole-body control, the authors introduce a Behavior World Model that jointly predicts the next action, the next state, and the next feasible behavior distribution instead of merely mimicking reference motions. A single unified policy achieves contact interaction with steps and chairs, safe shrinkage under physically implausible commands, and self-recovery from falls.
hero_caption: Overall system overview of GigaBrain-WBC-0.5. 3D contact geometry is automatically annotated from motion data to build the training environment. A Causal Transformer-based world model jointly predicts joint commands, next states, and next behavior distributions, enabling high-precision whole-body tracking on real robots, environment contact, fall recovery, and cross-embodiment transfer.
overview:
In recent humanoid control, imitation learning over massive human motion datasets has become the mainstream paradigm to consolidate diverse skills—such as running, jumping, and standing up—into a single policy. However, most prior research assumes flat, featureless ground. Consequently, when contact with the environment occurs, such as sitting on a chair or stepping onto a ledge, these controllers suffer sharp shifts in dynamics and readily fail.

To tackle this, the authors conceived treating the robot not merely as a passive motion tracker, but as a Behavior World Model that implicitly captures what states and behavioral options its actions will produce next. Specifically, they built an automatic annotation pipeline that evaluates kinematic ground contact from standard motion capture data to reconstruct 3D obstacle geometry such as chairs and stairs, generating large-scale interaction data. A Transformer model is then trained to jointly predict the current control action, the next proprioceptive state, and a mixture distribution of next feasible latent behaviors.

Evaluated in simulation and on real hardware (Unitree G1 and Maker L01), this approach substantially outperformed existing large-scale flat-ground trackers. The success rate on tasks involving contact with ledges or platforms leaped 4.3x from the best baseline's ~19% to 81.3%. When subjected to physically implausible, impossible motion commands, the policy did not freeze; instead, it automatically projected the commands into a best-effort motion, maintaining an 83.1% survival rate. Furthermore, its recovery rate from fallen states reached 99.3%.

These results demonstrate that even when a human operator supplies coarse motion commands via VR goggles, the robot can intelligently brace its body against environmental geometry, yielding an exceptionally robust whole-body control interface that tenaciously weathers external disturbances and unreasonable commands.
contributions: Formulating the whole-body control policy as a Causal Transformer that jointly predicts the action, next state, and next latent behavior distribution, creating a Behavior World Model that captures environment dynamics.
Developing an annotation pipeline that detects foot and body contact traces from motion kinematics to automatically reconstruct 3D support geometry directly loadable into simulators.

Proposing a stateless geometric filter that reuses the world model's own predicted behavior distribution to smoothly project out-of-distribution, implausible commands to the nearest feasible action online.

Integrating fall recovery directly into the same policy rather than treating it as a separate operational mode, demonstrating outstanding environmental adaptability and disturbance resilience in simulation and on real hardware (G1, L01).

sections.heading: Leaving flat ground behind: whole-body control that touches the world
sections.summary: Existing large-scale whole-body motion trackers function only on flat ground and fail under dynamic changes caused by contact with steps or chairs. This work introduces GigaBrain-WBC-0.5, a world model that predicts its own future behaviors to handle environmental interactions, unreasonable commands, and falls.
sections.details:
The true value of humanoid robots lies in their ability to use their entire bodies to work in complex environments designed for humans. In recent whole-body control (WBC), large-scale trackers trained with reinforcement learning across tens of thousands of motion clips have emerged to handle walking, squatting, dancing, and more within a single policy. These models serve as exceptional low-level interfaces that absorb balance and physical consistency when a VR operator or a high-level Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model issues coarse commands.

However, conventional trackers carry a critical weakness: they are trained exclusively on bare, flat ground. When a robot sits on a chair, carries a heavy load, or places a foot on a step, the height of reaction forces and the center of mass shift fundamentally. Existing methods can neither recognize nor exploit these dynamics changes. The primary culprit is the severe lack of paired datasets combining 3D scene geometry with whole-body motions.

Command robustness poses an even trickier problem. On flat ground, scaling up training data can prevent the robot from falling under wild commands, but once an environment is introduced, motions that are feasible on flat terrain may become physically impossible on stairs. Because the set of executable actions becomes environment-conditioned, simply scaling data is insufficient.

To overcome this, this study proposes a Causal Transformer—a Behavior World Model—that outputs control actions while jointly predicting the robot's next physical state and the distribution of next feasible action commands. Combined with an automatic annotation pipeline that reconstructs 3D contact geometry from standard motion data and an online filter that uses predicted distributions to pull implausible commands into safe bounds, the authors realize a single whole-body control policy uniting environmental contact with ultimate robustness.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of large-scale motion tracking and contact control
sections.summary: This section surveys two historically separate threads: large-scale imitation-based flat trackers and specialized terrain controllers. The proposed method distinguishes itself by embracing environmental contact across all degrees of freedom and unifying fall recovery into a single model.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main categories.

### Whole-Body Motion Trackers and Behavior Foundation Models
Approaches that imitate massive amounts of MoCap (motion capture) data to construct a single policy, such as SONIC, HoloMotion-1, and Humanoid-GPT, are progressing rapidly. However, because they are trained in flat, empty scenes, they lack the ability to touch objects other than the floor. Furthermore, researchers have noted a generalization ceiling where broadening motion coverage degrades tracking precision.

### Whole-Body Control Interacting with Terrains and Objects
Studies also exist on traversing stairs and rough terrain, parkour control, and large-object manipulation. Yet many of these are locomotion-centric controllers accepting only root velocity commands, making them unsuitable as real-time whole-body teleoperation interfaces for the upper body and arms. While some prior works jointly handle motion and scenes (such as SceneBot), they are often limited to 2.5D elevation maps or require explicit per-link contact flags, constraining operator freedom.

### Robustness to Out-of-Distribution Commands and Falls
Prior literature has explored constraining commands to safe envelopes or deploying dedicated stand-up recovery controllers (like HoST). However, switching to a specialized recovery policy every time the robot falls interrupts the operator's ongoing task. In this work, standing up is learned as just another motion within the tracker itself, and the world model's own predicted distribution is used to project wild commands safely online without needing extra classifiers.

sections.heading: The behavior world model and automatic 3D terrain generation
sections.summary: Targeting a 29-DoF humanoid, reference motions are embedded into a latent space and passed to a Causal Transformer that jointly predicts actions, next states, and next behavior distributions (GMM). This is paired with automatic 3D geometry extraction and a closed-form safety projection filter.
sections.details:
The core designs and algorithms of this method are detailed below.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The robot used is the Unitree G1 (29 DoF) running PD control at 50 Hz. Policy inputs consist of proprioception $\bm{s}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{67}$ (gravity vector, angular velocities, joint positions/velocities), the previous action $\bm{a}_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{29}$, and a 10-frame future reference motion window $\bm{c}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{440}$.

### 3.2 Behavior World Model Architecture
The reference motion window $\bm{c}_t$ undergoes noise addition and masking before an MLP encoder converts it into a 64-dimensional raw latent command $\bm{z}_t^{\mathrm{raw}}$. Crucially, during training only, a Finite Scalar Quantizer (FSQ: discretizing space onto a grid) and a decoder form a reconstruction loop. This encourages the latent space to disperse smoothly without collapsing into narrow dimensions, making subsequent modeling with Gaussian mixture models straightforward.

The network backbone is a 6-layer Causal Transformer (local attention window of 32 frames with KV caching). Its final hidden state feeds three heads:
- **Policy Head**: joint target positions $\bm{a}_t$
- **State Prediction Head**: next physical state $\bm{s}_{t+1}$
- **Behavior Head**: predicted distribution of the next latent command $\mathcal{G}_{t+1}$ (a 4-component diagonal-covariance GMM)

Predicting the next state grounds contact forces into the internal representation, while predicting the next command distribution allows the model to inherently understand what actions are feasible next in the current terrain and environment.

### 3.3 Automatic 3D Terrain Annotation
To reconstruct environment geometry from ordinary MoCap data, surface points on contact links (such as feet) are kinematically replayed in MuJoCo. Timesteps where velocity falls below a threshold and normal deceleration exceeds a set value are flagged as contacts and accumulated into a 3D point cloud. After passing through a penetration filter against the full robot body to retain only non-colliding points, DBSCAN clustering groups them into 3D box primitives (chairs, stair treads, boxes).

### 3.4 Online Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Command Filtering
At deployment, the latent command $\bm{z}_t^{\mathrm{raw}}$ is evaluated against the Gaussian mixture $\mathcal{G}_{t-1}$ predicted in the previous step using Mahalanobis distance. After identifying the most likely component $k^{\star}$, if the distance exceeds a safety radius $R_{\mathrm{safe}}$, the vector is scaled radially back toward the center $\bm{\mu}_{k^{\star}}$. Rather than halting, the robot carries out a best-effort execution that preserves the original intent as closely as possible. Computational cost is under 1 ms, and the safety radius can be tuned via a single scalar at runtime.

### 3.5 Training Pipeline
Reinforcement learning is performed using PPO in Isaac Lab. Training incorporates fall recovery curricula alongside random disturbance forces applied to the wrists and torso. Furthermore, the trained weights can be transferred to a different embodiment (Maker L01) with straightforward fine-tuning.

sections.heading: Withstanding unseen obstacles, impossible commands, and violent falls
sections.summary: In MuJoCo sim-to-sim evaluations, the method achieved an 81.3% success rate on terrain interaction, 83.1% survival under impossible commands, and a 99.3% fall recovery rate, vastly outperforming baselines like SONIC. Hardware experiments verified stair climbing, box carrying, and disturbance recovery.
sections.details:
The authors validated the method through simulation benchmarks and real-robot hardware experiments.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Baselines
The benchmark covers four regimes: flat-ground tracking (Standard), physically implausible motions (OOD), contact motions with stairs and furniture (Terrain), and recovery from fallen poses (Fall). Three state-of-the-art large-scale trackers—SONIC, HoloMotion-1, and Humanoid-GPT—served as baselines under identical sim-to-sim conditions in MuJoCo (full-trajectory replay, masking global root positions unobservable on real hardware).

### 4.2 Motion Tracking Performance Comparisons
- **Standard (Flat ground)**: InterTrack recorded a Mean Per-Keypoint Position Error (MPKPE) of 76.6 mm and a Success Rate (SR) of 96.3%, outperforming flat-ground-specialized baselines (SONIC: 82.3 mm, 94.1%).
- **Terrain (Contact interaction)**: While baselines treated contact as disturbance and collapsed to 14–19% success rates, the proposed method maintained an 81.3% success rate with an MPKPE of 93.3 mm (4.3x higher success and 3.0x lower error than the strongest baseline).
- **OOD (Implausible commands)**: Under impossible reference motions where baselines achieved only 50–70% survival, the online filter preserved an 83.1% survival rate while staying closest to the intended motion.
- **Fall (Recovery)**: Baselines struggled with recovery rates between 0.7% and 5.9% (flailing on the floor), whereas the proposed method reached a 99.3% recovery rate. It also yielded the smoothest joint motion with a jerk of 1050.6 $\mathrm{rad/s^3}$.

### 4.3 Environment Interaction and Real-Robot Validation
Human visual inspection confirmed that 92% of the automatically annotated terrain motions exhibited correct geometry. On the real Unitree G1, identical teleoperation commands caused SONIC to freeze mid-air over a box, whereas the proposed method leaned into the box to sit down, climbed a step, and descended stairs while carrying a load.

### 4.4 Robustness and Cross-Embodiment Transfer
When a chair or platform was abruptly pulled away, the robot avoided emergency shutdowns or dropping its payload, instead smoothly transitioning into a stable best-effort posture. When kicked to the ground, it stood up naturally without switching controllers and resumed tracking. Furthermore, the G1 world model transferred to the Maker L01 via brief fine-tuning, successfully adapting to logistics and household tasks.

Across sitting on a box (a), ascending/descending steps (b), holding objects (c), lifting a fire extinguisher (d), and walking on steps while carrying a load (e), only the proposed method effectively utilizes contact forces to succeed.

(c) After being kicked down, it stands up smoothly under the same policy. (d, e) During a complex spin-kick command, enabling the filter (ON) preemptively prevents falls.

sections.heading: World models that understand their surroundings will redefine whole-body control
sections.summary: By predicting both actions and future states/behavior distributions, this Behavior World Model proves that terrain adaptability and disturbance robustness can coexist in a single policy. Future extensions include reconstructing non-contact geometry and estimating physical risk directly.
sections.details:
This work presented GigaBrain-WBC-0.5, a behavior world model for humanoid whole-body control. It demonstrated that missing elements in conventional trackers—environmental contact and resilience against impossible commands—can be solved in a unified manner by having the controller predict its own future (next states and next behavior distributions).

Combining an automatic 3D terrain reconstruction pipeline with a closed-form online projection filter based on predicted distributions, the method dominated baselines in simulated terrain adaptation (81.3% success), implausible command survival (83.1%), and fall recovery (99.3%), while proving its tenacity in real-world deployments.

The authors also outline several limitations. The online filter was primarily verified in simulation, and the safety radius $R_{\mathrm{safe}}$ currently requires tuning across robot embodiments or checkpoints. In addition, hazard avoidance is probabilistic rather than an explicit mathematical optimization of physical damage risk, relying on similarity to training experiences. Finally, terrain reconstruction only captures surfaces the body physically contacted, leaving untouched obstacles invisible. Future work will investigate reconstructing non-contact geometry and directly mapping state predictions to physical risk metrics.

takeaways: Having a whole-body control policy jointly predict actions, next states, and next behavior distributions naturally embeds contact dynamics and environmental affordances into internal representations.
Standard motion capture data can yield high-quality 3D contact geometry by extracting kinematic contact and deceleration signals, unlocking scalable training for environment interaction.
The world model's own predicted next-step distribution (GMM) enables closed-form, best-effort online filtering of out-of-distribution commands without auxiliary classifiers.
Integrating fall recovery as a standard behavior within a single unified policy creates a robust teleoperation and whole-body control foundation that never interrupts ongoing tasks.
limitations: Automatic terrain annotation relies on contact traces left by the body, meaning untouched obstacles and complete surrounding geometry cannot be reconstructed.
The safety radius parameter in the online filter requires manual tuning per embodiment or checkpoint, and does not directly optimize against mathematical criteria for falls or physical damage.
Omitting absolute root position feedback introduces a slight trade-off where flat-ground root velocity tracking is marginally less accurate than some baseline models.
